## Derivatives
Instantaneous Rate of Change of f at t = a =
$\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}$
The derivative of f at a, written f'(a), is defined as:
$f^{'}(a)=\lim_{h\to0} \left(\frac{f(a+h)-f(a)}{h}\right)$
If the limit exists then f is said to be differentiable at a.
Read as f prime of a

The derivative of f at a is the slope of the tangent line to the graph f(x) at point (a, f(a))

Solve using the definition of a derivative means use the long way.
If it does not specify you can use the shortcut.

The derivative of a line with no slope is 0. (so a straight horizontal line)

Remember abs value functions are piecewise. When finding the dervivative, find the left and right hand side (if x is positive or negative). If they are not equal it is not defined. (typically, the derivative of the point the two \/ meet it is undefined since they are not equal, but anywhere else it is defined)

To find the function of a derivative, you can still use the same formula but without a specific point in x. You basically do the entire f(x) function once with x + h and the other just by itself.
Values are only valid for f'(x) functions if the x value is in the domain of f'(x), and only if the limit actually exists.
For example:
f(x) = x^2
f'(x) = lim(h -> 0) ((x + h)^2 - x^2) / h)
= (x^2 + 2xh + h^2 - x^2) / h
= (h(2x) + h^2) / h
= 2x + h
Since its lim rules itd be the lim (2x) + lim(h) = 2x
f'(x) = 2x

If f'(x) > 0 on an open interval I, then f(x) is increasing on I.
If f'(x) < 0 on an open interval I, then f(x) is decreasing on I.
If f'(x) = 0 on an open interval I, then f(x) is constant on I.

*Differentiation Formulas:*
- If f(x) = k with k constant, then f'(x) = 0
- If f(x) = mx + b, with m,b constant, then f'(x) = m
- *Power Rule*: If n != 0 and f(x) = x^n, then f(x) = nx^(n-1) <--- my best friend my favorite thing the best thing
Remember things in the denominator of functions can be moved to the top if you flip its exponent sign (the n in front of x will be opposite sign then too remember)

Note: You can estimate a derivative from a function table by finding the slope of the point directly to the left of point a, directly to the right, and averaging them

## Tangent Lines
To find the equation of tangents lines, take the derivative of the function at whatever x value given. This is the slope

Then, take the x given and put it back into the original function to get the y.

The coordinates + m in y = mx + b format is the equation for the tangent line.

Generalized, given a differentiable function f and a point (x, y), the equation for the tangent line to the function f at (x, y) is given by -

You can use tangent lines to approximate points on f(x). Like if you want to know f(-1.01) and f(x) = x^3 + 2x, the tangent line meets f(x) at f(-1). So, if you put -1.01 into the tangent line equation, its pretty close to the value of f(x) at -1.01.
